query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a rapid annealing treatment immediately after >50% hot or hybrid rolling will refine the dual-phase lamellar colonies in eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA, thereby simultaneously enhancing both its tensile strength and room‐temperature ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA produced by conventional thermomechanical processing that yields dual-phase lamellar colonies with inhomogeneous interfacial properties and residual stresses favoring microcrack initiation.
generation.intervention: Optimized post-hot rolling rapid annealing treatment
generation.conditions: Immediately after achieving >50% rolling reduction, heat the alloy at a rate of approximately 15 K/s to around 700 °C and hold for 30–50 seconds in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Refinement of the lamellar colony microstructure and enhanced interlamellar interface quality through stress relief and partial ordering or recrystallization at the colony boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The rapid annealing relieves residual stresses and promotes partial recrystallization/ordering at phase boundaries, which reduces microstructural inhomogeneities that act as sites for microcrack nucleation. This processing step preserves fine grain sizes to maintain strength while improving the toughness of interfaces, thereby enabling both higher yield strength and enhanced ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unannealed conventional lamellar baseline, the treated alloy will exhibit a statistically significant increase in tensile yield strength and ductility at room temperature due to a more uniform and refined microstructure.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA with dual-phase lamellar colonies that are prone to microcrack initiation due to residual stresses and poorly conditioned interlamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only when the rolling reduction is substantial (greater than 50%) and the annealing parameters (temperature, heating rate, and duration) are maintained within the specified window; deviations (such as over-annealing) may lead to grain coarsening and counteract strength improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in strength and ductility are uncertain and require experimental validation; the optimal annealing duration and temperature window may also vary slightly with processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA samples via hot or hybrid rolling with >50% reduction. Subject one set to the rapid annealing treatment (15 K/s ramp to ~700 °C, 30–50 s dwell) and leave the other set as the unannealed control. Perform room-temperature tensile tests and microstructural evaluations using SEM/TEM and EBSD to assess interlamellar boundary quality and grain size.
measurements: Grain size and interface characteristics (via microstructural imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in both strength and ductility compared to the control, or if microstructural evaluation fails to demonstrate improved interlamellar boundary properties (e.g., reduced residual stresses and refined colonies), then the hypothesis is falsified.

However, in our case, the formation of large cracks by the coalescence of small microcracks was found to be inhibited, even when some of the microcracks are separated by only a single lamella (Fig. 3b and Fig. 4b). To elucidate this phenomenon, further microstructure observations found that after the heavy-rolling deformation (84–86%), the resultant samples possess massive special lamellae (~82–87 vol.%) with a directionally aligned arrangement along the rolling direction (Supplementary Fig. 7). It should be noted that the aligned arrangement here does not refer to the orientation behavior as in crystallography. With their special lamellar architecture, the DPHL materials are akin to artificially fabricated laminated composites. The ductile components such as the FCC matrix, and even the hard B2 lamellae in the current samples, will therefore work well as very efficient crack arresters to delay crack propagation and coalescence during deformation: this is experimentally supported by the existence of restrained circle-like microcracks with blunted crack-tips (Fig. 4c, d). A novel hybrid processing strategy achieves a unique structural-compositional dual heterogeneous microstructure in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy resulting in unprecedented strength (>2000 MPa) and ductility (~8%) combination.

Two types of rolling processes were performed; the first was cold rolling 70% (CR70), and the second was hot rolling 50% followed by cold rolling 70% (HR50CR70). During CR70, an ingot is rolled at room temperature with a deformation strain of 70%. During HR50CR70, an ingot is heated in the furnace at 1000 °C for 1 h and then rolled with a 50% strain. After a hot-rolled sample is cooled down to room temperature, it is then rolled at room temperature with a deformation strain of 70%. In addition, rapid annealing was performed in the present study. The effects of rapid annealing (heating rate of 15 °C/s) under various annealing durations (30, 40, 50, and 60 s) were examined to study the recrystallization sequence of MEAs and explore the relationship between their microstructure and mechanical properties.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy based on AlCoCrFeNi (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1)
proposals.intervention: Hydrogen charging at controlled low concentrations
proposals.conditions: Expose the as-cast and hot-rolled alloy to a dilute hydrogen atmosphere (targeting ~50–100 ppm dissolved hydrogen) at room temperature prior to tensile testing
proposals.structural_mediator: Hydrogen-induced reduction of the stacking fault energy and promotion of reversible nanotwinning along lamellar colony boundaries
proposals.mechanism: Hydrogen alloying lowers the barrier for twin nucleation in the dual-phase lamellae; the resultant nanotwins act as in situ obstacles to dislocation propagation while simultaneously deflecting or arresting microcrack initiation and coalescence along the numerous internal boundaries
proposals.predicted_outcome: Both yield strength and tensile ductility are improved relative to the unmodified lamellar baseline, with enhanced work-hardening and delayed localization of strain-induced microcracks
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By inducing beneficial nanotwinning without resorting to additional phases or complex processing, this single chemical intervention leverages an intrinsic change in defect-mediated deformation and crack arresting at the internal boundaries

proposals.intervention: Microalloying with a small addition of Zr (approx. 5–7 at.%)
proposals.conditions: Introduce Zr during arc-melting followed by standard casting and a rapid annealing treatment at ~850 °C for a brief period to maximize Zr segregation at lamellar interfaces
proposals.structural_mediator: Segregation of large Zr atoms to colony interfaces, leading to local lattice distortions and enhanced interfacial bonding/coherency
proposals.mechanism: The Zr-induced lattice distortion increases the interfacial strength by reducing free-boundary energy and stabilizes the dual-phase lamellar structure, while also contributing to solid solution strengthening within the lamellae
proposals.predicted_outcome: An alloy exhibiting higher yield strength and improved tensile ductility compared to the baseline due to reinforced colony boundaries that are less susceptible to microcrack nucleation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single compositional intervention directly targets the interfacial vulnerabilities in the lamellar colonies by thermodynamically stabilizing and mechanically toughening the internal boundaries

proposals.intervention: Optimized post-hot rolling rapid annealing treatment
proposals.conditions: Apply a rapid thermal annealing cycle (e.g., heating at ~15 K/s to ~700 °C for 30–50 seconds) immediately following a substantial (>50%) reduction via hot or hybrid rolling
proposals.structural_mediator: Refinement of the lamellar colony microstructure and promotion of a uniformly distributed, fine-scale duplex structure with controlled interlamellar boundary properties
proposals.mechanism: The short annealing treatment allows stress relief and partial ordering (or even slight transformation) at the colony interfaces, reducing microstructural inhomogeneities and residual stresses that catalyze microcrack formation, while concurrently preserving fine grain sizes for strength
proposals.predicted_outcome: The annealed alloy is expected to exhibit an enhanced combination of strength and ductility compared to the unannealed, conventionally processed lamellar baseline due to improved interfacial toughness
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single thermomechanical processing step reconditions the internal boundaries to resist microcracking while also refining the structure for enhanced strength, providing an integrated pathway to overcome the traditional trade-off

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi)
proposals.intervention: Deposition of a nanoscale, ductile interlamellar coating via atomic layer deposition (ALD)
proposals.conditions: After casting and coarse lamellar formation, apply an ALD process to deposit a ~10 nm-thick, conformal metallic (e.g., Ni or Cu) film selectively concentrating at the colony boundaries under low-temperature conditions (<200 °C)
proposals.structural_mediator: A continuous, nanoscale interfacial metallic layer along lamellar boundaries
proposals.mechanism: The interlamellar coating acts as an effective crack arrester and reinforces the weak interfaces by providing enhanced interfacial bonding and residual compressive stresses, thereby mitigating the initiation and propagation of microcracks during tensile deformation
proposals.predicted_outcome: The presence of the ductile interfacial layer is predicted to raise both the overall tensile strength and the ductility of the alloy relative to the untreated lamellar baseline by bridging cracks and redistributing local stresses
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This single surface modification intervention directly addresses the microcracking problem at the most vulnerable sites—the interlamellar boundaries—without altering the bulk composition, thus potentially bypassing the conventional strength-ductility trade-off

critiques.addresses_problem: The intervention targets the key issue by reinforcing the weak colony boundaries via Zr segregation, potentially reducing microcrack nucleation.
critiques.constraints: It respects the material system (AlCoCrFeNi2.1) and operates under standard casting and annealing conditions, but there is a risk of inadvertently altering the phase balance if Zr forms brittle intermetallics.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of using a larger atomic species (Zr) to induce lattice distortion and reinforce interfaces is physically plausible. However, the supporting evidence is mainly for interstitial effects (e.g., oxygen) rather than microalloying with Zr, so the translation isn’t entirely direct.
critiques.feasibility: Arc-melting with microalloying and subsequent rapid annealing is an established method in alloy processing, though controlling Zr segregation without forming unwanted phases may be challenging.
critiques.evidence: The literature (e.g., PMC9925791, PMC5227964, PMC6175879) provides indirect support for improved interfacial strength via lattice distortions, yet does not specifically document Zr additions in this HEA system.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is the potential formation of brittle Zr-rich intermetallic phases instead of the desired interfacial segregation, which could worsen the ductility.
critiques.fix: Optimize the annealing schedule (time and temperature) to promote Zr segregation at lamellar boundaries while avoiding the precipitation of brittle intermetallic phases.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction directly tackles the microcracking issue by thermally reconditioning the colony interfaces and refining the microstructure, which is central to the problem.
critiques.constraints: The approach uses optimized post-hot rolling rapid annealing within the accepted processing window and does not sacrifice the inherent phase structure of the alloy.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism of stress relief, controlled recrystallization, and microstructural refinement is well-established and sound, promoting both strength and ductility.
critiques.feasibility: Rapid annealing and thermomechanical treatments are standard in alloy processing, making the intervention highly feasible with existing methods.
critiques.evidence: Multiple studies (e.g., PMC9506522, PMC6353877, PMC6687781) support the benefits of rapid annealing on similar HEA systems, linking refined interfaces with improved mechanical properties.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is potential over-annealing, which could lead to excessive grain growth and a loss of the desired strength.
critiques.fix: Implement precise control of the annealing duration and temperature to ensure adequate stress relief and microstructural refinement while preventing overgrowth.

critiques.addresses_problem: The strategy aims to improve the weak interlamellar boundaries by depositing a ductile nanoscale coating, which conceptually targets the microcracking issue at its origin.
critiques.constraints: While the use of ALD at low temperatures is aligned with maintaining the bulk properties, the intervention assumes selective deposition on internal boundaries—a challenging prospect given the alloy’s cast microstructure.
critiques.physical_soundness: Although deposition of thin films via ALD is physically sound on exposed surfaces, achieving a conformal, selective coating on internal colony boundaries in a bulk cast material raises concerns regarding coating uniformity and adhesion.
critiques.feasibility: ALD is established for coating applications; however, applying it to internal interfaces of a non-porous, dense material may not be straightforward without additional pre-treatment steps.
critiques.evidence: Relevant studies (e.g., PMC6353877, PMC6478865, PMC4682111) discuss microcrack arresting via interfacial modifications, but they do not specifically support the feasibility of an ALD-based approach for internal boundaries in this system.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that ALD may not effectively penetrate and uniformly coat the internal lamellar boundaries, potentially leaving the critical sites unprotected.
critiques.fix: Incorporate a pre-treatment (such as controlled etching or creating microcrack networks) to expose the internal colony boundaries, thereby enhancing the likelihood of a conformal and uniform ALD coating.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction addresses the brittle behavior by attempting to induce beneficial nanotwinning at the lamellar boundaries through controlled hydrogen charging.
critiques.constraints: The method complies with the specified operating conditions by using low hydrogen concentrations; however, it must be carefully controlled to avoid detrimental hydrogen embrittlement.
critiques.physical_soundness: Lowering the stacking fault energy via hydrogen to promote nanotwinning is a mechanism supported by previous studies and is physically plausible, although its effectiveness in this specific HEA may vary.
critiques.feasibility: Hydrogen charging under controlled conditions is a well-known method, but achieving a homogeneous, low-level hydrogen incorporation without triggering embrittlement is challenging.
critiques.evidence: Studies (e.g., PMC5575320 and related records) show that hydrogen can enhance nanotwinning and work hardening in HEAs, though these experiments primarily involve different compositions.
critiques.main_risk: The key risk lies in potentially inducing hydrogen embrittlement or non-uniform hydrogen distribution, which could worsen the alloy’s ductility instead of improving it.
critiques.fix: Refine the hydrogen charging parameters (e.g., concentration, duration, and charging method) to ensure a uniform distribution while preventing localized embrittlement.
